--- title: "LFP Compression: Tuning an Intermediate Tier" description: "Three sweeps across the 11 benchmark recordings (alpha only, epsilon only, and both jointly) to find a decoding-aware intermediate compression tier between the shipped default and aggressive passes." date: "2026-08-31" author: "Olivier Winter" categories: [electrophysiology, LFP, compression, Neuropixels, decoding] --- ## Overview [decoding_validation.qmd](decoding_validation.qmd) showed the shipped aggressive tier (ε=450, α=96) measurably hurts decoding — feedback especially — with no warning from RMSE, the metric it was calibrated on, and proposed retiring it in favour of a decoding-aware intermediate tier. This page runs that search across the same 11 benchmark recordings, all three decode targets (wheel speed, choice, feedback), and lands on a single recommendation. **Bottom line: there is no free intermediate tier.** Sweeping α alone (ε=150 fixed) or ε alone (α=28 fixed) both leave the compression ratio essentially flat while decoding keeps eroding — neither parameter is a usable lever on its own. Only scaling **both together** traces a real trade-off curve, and on that curve, moving *any* distance from the current default costs real feedback-decoding fidelity from the first step, with no favourable "knee." **Recommendation: keep the shipped default (ε=150, α=28) as the cohort-wide tier**; if more compression is required, ε=250/α=50 (~104× realized, vs default's 87×) is the only non-dominated compromise found — a real, disclosed cost (feedback retention 0.575 vs default's 0.597), not a free win. Retire the aggressive tier either way: it is not on the useful part of the curve for decoding-sensitive downstream use. ## Method Same pipeline as [decoding_validation.qmd](decoding_validation.qmd#method): band-power envelope features (log Hilbert amplitude, delta/theta/beta/gamma, 96 channels), RidgeCV for wheel speed (R²), standardized LogisticRegressionCV for choice/feedback (balanced accuracy, 5-fold CV, simple per-fold label-shuffle null). Each compression tier is a fresh `lfpack.compress_to_h5` build from the same Cadzow-denoised checkpoint (`lf_resampled_car_cadzow.npy`) used throughout the SVD benchmark, so tiers differ only in (ε, α) — no other pipeline stage changes. Three sweeps, in the order they were actually run (each motivated by what the previous one found): 1. **α only**, ε=150 fixed: α ∈ {28 (default), 40, 55, 70, 75, 80, 85, 90, 96}. 2. **ε only**, α=28 fixed: ε ∈ {150 (default), 225, 300, 375, 450}. 3. **Diagonal**: (ε, α) scaled together along the line from default (150, 28) to the shipped aggressive point (450, 96): (250, 50) and (350, 75). Every sweep also reports each tier's on-disk file size (summed across the 11 recordings) and channel-averaged Welch PSD, to check the high-frequency roll-off directly rather than infer it from RMSE. ## Sweep 1: alpha alone doesn't buy compression ::: {#35fd1d9b .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
r2_wheel balanced_accuracy_choice balanced_accuracy_feedback cr_realized
tier

alpha28 (default) 0.127 0.563 0.597 86.679
alpha40 0.122 0.560 0.584 82.420
alpha55 0.116 0.553 0.569 88.756
alpha70 0.111 0.550 0.562 93.080
alpha75 0.110 0.549 0.559 94.279
alpha80 0.108 0.552 0.556 95.310
alpha85 0.106 0.549 0.556 96.220
alpha90 0.106 0.552 0.556 97.085
alpha96 (eps150) 0.104 0.552 0.555 97.974
``` ::: ::: ![Alpha sweep (ε=150 fixed): wheel R², choice/feedback balanced accuracy, and total file size (with realized CR labelled), 11 recordings, one box per tier.](figures/2026-08-31_alpha_sweep_decoding_summary_full.png){.lightbox} ![Median channel-averaged PSD, alpha sweep. Curves fan out cleanly in beta/gamma as α rises — real high-frequency loss — but see below: it doesn't shrink the files.](figures/2026-08-31_alpha_sweep_psd_full.png){.lightbox} Raising α from 28 to 96 moves total file size from 0.242 GB to 0.211 GB across the 11 recordings — a 13% reduction, realized CR 87×→98×. Feedback balanced accuracy over the same range drops from a mean retained fraction of 0.688 to 0.388 (chance-corrected against uncompressed). The PSD figure confirms α *is* removing real high-frequency content the whole way — it just isn't buying proportional storage savings once ε is fixed. **α outside its calibrated default is a real cost for negligible benefit.** ## Sweep 2: epsilon alone doesn't buy compression either ::: {#9cb7d0a1 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
r2_wheel balanced_accuracy_choice balanced_accuracy_feedback cr_realized
tier
uncompressed 0.139 0.564 0.642 1.000
alpha28 (default) 0.127 0.563 0.597 86.679
eps225 (alpha28) 0.125 0.561 0.593 82.709
eps300 (alpha28) 0.124 0.563 0.591 89.387
eps375 (alpha28) 0.123 0.558 0.584 94.897
eps450 (alpha28) 0.122 0.555 0.585 99.948
``` ::: ::: ![Epsilon sweep (α=28 fixed): same layout as above.](figures/2026-08-31_epsilon_sweep_decoding_summary.png){.lightbox} ![Median channel-averaged PSD, epsilon sweep.](figures/2026-08-31_epsilon_sweep_psd.png){.lightbox} Same story: total size only drops from 0.242 GB (ε=150) to 0.211 GB (ε=450) — 87×→100× realized — while feedback retention falls from 0.688 to 0.603. **The most striking number here isn't in either table: `eps450 (alpha28)` is 0.211 GB at 100× realized CR, but the shipped aggressive tier — same ε=450, but α=96 instead of 28 — is 0.098 GB at 217× realized CR.** Same rank truncation, more than double the compression, purely from raising α. That contradicts sweep 1, where raising α at ε=150 barely moved the needle. **ε and α interact**: α's leverage over file size depends on ε, and vice versa. Neither axis is a free-standing lever — the compression payoff only appears when both are pushed together, which is exactly what the two-tier design (default vs. aggressive) already does, just as a single large jump with nothing in between. ## Sweep 3: the diagonal — where the real trade-off lives ::: {#9d9afa23 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
r2_wheel balanced_accuracy_choice balanced_accuracy_feedback cr cr_realized total_GB
tier
uncompressed 0.139 0.564 0.642 1.000 1.000 20.402
alpha28 (default) 0.127 0.563 0.597 100.815 86.679 0.242
eps250/alpha50 0.117 0.552 0.575 159.565 103.736 0.201
eps350/alpha75 0.109 0.549 0.558 220.118 128.251 0.163
aggressive (eps450, alpha96, shipped) 0.104 0.552 0.557 280.887 217.478 0.098
``` ::: ::: ![Diagonal sweep (ε and α scaled together, from default to the shipped aggressive point): the real Pareto curve.](figures/2026-08-31_diagonal_sweep_decoding_summary.png){.lightbox} ![Median channel-averaged PSD, diagonal sweep — cleanly ordered by compression level.](figures/2026-08-31_diagonal_sweep_psd.png){.lightbox} This is the real trade-off curve: realized CR climbs steadily (87× → 104× → 128× → 217×) as total size falls (0.242 → 0.201 → 0.163 → 0.098 GB), and feedback balanced accuracy declines in step (mean retained fraction 0.688 → 0.530 → 0.410 → 0.402). Two things stand out: - **No favourable knee.** The curve declines continuously and immediately from the very first step away from default — there's no point where a chunk of compression is "free." Choosing an intermediate tier is choosing how much feedback fidelity to spend, not finding a shortcut past that cost. - **`eps350/alpha75` is dominated by the shipped aggressive tier.** It costs almost the same feedback retention (0.410 vs. aggressive's 0.402) for barely half the compression (128× vs. 217×). If more compression than `eps250/alpha50` is ever acceptable, there is no reason to stop at `eps350/alpha75` — go straight to aggressive. ## Recommendation For the full ephys-atlas cohort compression run: - **Default (ε=150, α=28) stays the standard tier.** No tested point clears even a modest (85%) retained-decoding bar relative to uncompressed, and default is the only tier that gets close (0.688 on the binding feedback constraint). - **If additional storage savings are required, use ε=250, α=50** — the only non-dominated intermediate point found (~104× realized CR, ~17% smaller than default's already-small footprint) at a real, disclosed cost (feedback retention drops to 0.575 from default's 0.597 in absolute terms, 0.530 vs. 0.688 chance-corrected). Do not use `eps350/alpha75` — it is dominated by the existing aggressive tier. - **Retire the current aggressive tier (ε=450, α=96)** for decoding-sensitive downstream use, per [decoding_validation.qmd](decoding_validation.qmd). It remains a legitimate choice *only* if ~104× (ε=250/α=50) isn't enough compression and the feedback-decoding cost of going all the way to ~217× is explicitly accepted — but nothing between `eps250/alpha50` and aggressive is worth shipping. **Practical note for the cluster run:** every tier here was built with `lfpack.compress_to_h5` directly from the existing `lf_resampled_car_cadzow.npy` Cadzow checkpoints already on disk for the 11 benchmark recordings (build cost ≈10-60s/recording per tier; no re-download or re-denoising needed). The same call — `compress_to_h5(cadzow_npy, out_h5, recording=pid, epsilon=250.0, alpha=50.0, fs=250.0, ...)` — is what should run per-recording on the full cohort if the ε=250/α=50 tier is adopted.
